inline.s: Dingmao wished to give up reciting the mantra and practice Buddha-recitation instead, and asked the Bodhisattva about it. The Bodhisattva said: "You wish to forsake the mantra and practice reciting the Buddha's name, single-mindedly devoted — nothing could be better. But you do not yet know the essentials of Buddha-recitation, so you can only be called a person who keeps the fasts and loves goodness, not yet a person who recites the Buddha's name. Why is this? To cross the great sea one must have a great boat; to gallop a thousand li one must choose a fine horse. Therefore a person who recites the Buddha's name must first possess great ability, cut off all entanglements, and break through the net of the world. Directly, the very recitation is the Buddha, the very Buddha is the mind — even beyond both forsaking and beyond affirming, one suddenly enters the Tathagata's great treasury of light. Only then is it called right-mindfulness Buddha-recitation, and only then may one be called a person who recites the Buddha's name. You should understand this meaning well."
[The net of the world]
People in this world are bound by all kinds of constraints, like fish in a net, hence it is called the net of the world.

Four young monks then came to call on the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said: "O young ones, from beginningless time sentient beings have, because of love and affection, become family and kin. And among kin, parents toward their children hold the heaviest grace and the keenest love, hard to cut and hard to let go. Now you have left the world, that is, you are fully ordained as monks; you should know that toward you your parents have a grace upon grace, beyond words
(beyond what speech can express)

. Therefore you should seize the vigor of this prime of life to diligently advance on the Way, and repay your parents' whole-hearted resolve in first cutting off affection and severing love — only then will you be worthy of these two words 'left the world.' If you instead give yourselves over to indulgence and sloth, so that your whole life comes to waste and decline
(so that your whole life ruins your practice of the Way and falls back)
, then this is the unfilial among the unfilial, a most grievous sinner under heaven. Because of my words, you should be stirred to deep and urgent reflection."

Four young monks came to call on the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said: "O young ones, from beginningless time sentient beings have, because of love and affection, become family and kin. And among kin, parents toward their children hold the heaviest grace and the keenest love, hard to cut and hard to let go. Now that you have left the world and have become monks, you should know that toward you your parents have a grace upon grace, which speech cannot express. Therefore you should seize the vigor of this prime of life to diligently advance on the Way, and repay your parents' whole-hearted resolve in first cutting off affection and severing love in sending you forth — only then will you be worthy of these two words 'left the world.' If you give yourselves over to indulgence and sloth, so that your whole life ruins your practice of the Way and falls back, then you are the unfilial among the unfilial, a most grievous sinner under heaven. Hearing these words of mine, you should be stirred to deep and urgent reflection."

The Bodhisattva again instructed the assembly, saying: "O good men, this body of a person is born of parents, nurtured by parents. All the manifold schemes in which you are now engaged, and all the manifold enjoyments — even if your parents gave you not a single coin, it is still your parents who gave birth to this body of yours, and so you have what you have today. Of all things the body is foremost; the body is the root. Pushing back from the root, is this not a parent's grace hard to speak of and hard to exhaust? Therefore the Buddha said: 'Even to utter one harsh, heavy word to one's parents brings measureless offense.' How much the more so those who do worse than this today? If one were to say that parents, by treating one unbearably, compel one to argue back, then one looks upon one's parents as strangers. One should only accept it with joy and compliance; your parents will have their own day of awakening. Never must you strive to prove you are right and others wrong, to become a man who rebels against heaven and violates the bonds of humanity."

The Bodhisattva again instructed the assembly, saying: "O good men, this body of a person is born of parents and nurtured by parents. All the manifold schemes in which you are now engaged, and all the manifold enjoyments — even if your parents gave you not a single coin, it is still your parents who gave birth to this body, so you have today. Of all things the body is foremost, and the body is the root. Pushing back from the root, is this not a parent's grace hard to speak of and hard to exhaust? Therefore the Buddha said: 'Even to utter one harsh, heavy word to one's parents still brings measureless offense.' How much the more those who do worse than this today? If one were to say that parents, by treating one unbearably, compel one to argue back, then one looks upon one's parents as strangers. You should only accept it with joy and compliance; your parents will have their own day of awakening. Never must you strive to argue who is wrong and who is right, to become a man who rebels against heaven and violates the bonds of humanity."

The Bodhisattva said: "O disciples, you should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the mind of sentient beings, and the sentient beings of the ten directions are the mind of the Buddhas. Therefore, when one recollects the Buddha and recites the Buddha, the Buddhas of the ten directions appear within your mind. Yet it is not that the Buddhas enter your mind, nor that your mind issues forth from the Buddhas; all of this is the fundamental enlightenment, wondrous and inherently bright, beyond thought."

The Bodhisattva said: "O disciples, you should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the mind of sentient beings, and the sentient beings of the ten directions are the mind of the Buddhas. Therefore, when one recollects the Buddha and recites the Buddha, the Buddhas of the ten directions appear within your mind. And yet it is not that the Buddhas enter your mind, nor that your mind issues forth from the Buddhas; all of this is the fundamental enlightenment, wondrous and inherently bright, beyond thought."

The Bodhisattva said: "When the activity of the mind ceases, that is the Buddhas' ever-abiding true mind; where the activity of the mind is present, that is the karmic mind of birth and death of sentient beings. Between the two there is not the space of a hair's breadth. If you can work at it closely and continuously, leaving not the slightest gap in this mind, only then will you obtain some measure of response. Do not, after doing a little half a year or ten months, say that I am able to discipline my mind in the Way — little do you know that this is precisely the place that obstructs the Way. Heed this well!"

The Bodhisattva instructed: "Where the activity of the mind ceases, that is the Buddhas' ever-abiding true mind; where the activity of the mind is present, that is the karmic mind of birth and death of sentient beings. Between the two there is not the space of a hair's breadth. If you can work at it closely and diligently, leaving not a single gap in this mind, only then will you obtain some measure of response. Do not, after a bit of a half year or ten months, say that I am able to discipline my mind in the Way — little do you know that this is precisely the place that obstructs the Way. Heed this well!"

blocks.text: A Wall of Bronze and Iron

inline.s: Again, although one has applied effort, if one has not yet reached the place of a wall of bronze and iron that cannot be pushed over or moved, then it is still not blended into one piece. Do not, upon seeing some slight sign, immediately stop, for this is a ruin on the half road
(the same as 'halfway')

, and will surely discard all one's previous effort, with no benefit at all. This is again a great sickness of students of the Way, and one must know it. You should understand that the Buddha-Dharma is like the great sea — the deeper you go, the deeper it becomes; it is by no means something a small view can exhaust. You should cultivate throughout your whole life, and make reaching the summit
(arriving at the highest point)
your standard; never take it as an easy matter."

Again, although one's effort advances, if one has not yet reached the place of a wall of bronze and iron that cannot be pushed over or moved, then it is still not blended into one piece. Do not, upon seeing some little result, immediately stop — this is to abandon the task halfway, and will surely discard all one's previous effort with no benefit at all. This is again a great sickness of students of the Way, and one must know it. You should understand that the Buddha-Dharma is like the great sea — the deeper you enter, the deeper it becomes; it is by no means something a small view can exhaust. You should cultivate throughout your whole life to the end, and make climbing to the summit your standard; never take it as an easy matter."

The Bodhisattva said: "The Samadhi of Buddha-recitation is accomplished by the great power of your own mind, not by anything else. That you now, in reciting the Buddha, are not the same day and night, and that stray thoughts still intermittently intrude — this is exactly the place where your mind does not apply force."

The Bodhisattva said: "The Samadhi of Buddha-recitation is accomplished by the great power of your own mind, and not by anything else. That you now, in reciting the Buddha, are not the same day and night, and that stray thoughts still interpose — this is exactly where the mind fails to apply force."

Gu Dingcheng sought instruction. The Bodhisattva said: "You have come to this monastery wishing to rely on the pure karma; do you know how one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?" He answered: "By reciting the Buddha's name, one is born there." The Bodhisattva said: "Do you know how one recites the Buddha's name and so gains rebirth?" He answered: "Holding fast to the name, single-minded and unconfused." The Bodhisattva said: "What is it to be single-minded and unconfused?" Dingcheng could not answer. The Bodhisattva said: "I know that you only
(only)
can speak these words, but may not yet be able to practice them in accord with the Dharma. Listen attentively to my words."

Gu Dingcheng sought instruction. The Bodhisattva said: "You have come to this monastery wishing to rely on the pure karma; do you know how one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?" Gu Dingcheng answered: "By reciting the Buddha's name, one is born there." The Bodhisattva said: "Do you know how one recites the Buddha's name and so gains rebirth?" Gu Dingcheng answered: "Holding fast to the name, single-minded and unconfused." The Bodhisattva asked: "What is it to be single-minded and unconfused?" Dingcheng could not answer. The Bodhisattva said: "I know that you can say 'Holding fast to the name, single-minded and unconfused, one gains rebirth,' yet may not be able to practice it in accord with the Dharma to the point of single-minded and unconfused. Gather your attention and listen attentively to my words."

O good man, the mind is originally without thought; thought pursues the imagined, and this imagined is false and unreal, and so one flows through birth and death. You should now know that this single phrase 'Amitabha Buddha' does not arise from imagination, does not exist from thought, dwells neither within nor without, and is without form or appearance. It is precisely to exhaust all false thinking. The Tathagatas, the Buddhas, are the pure, subtle, real body, neither one nor two, beyond discrimination. One who recites thus, with afflictions and dust-labor neither severed nor bound, is but the one mind. One must attain
(must)
single-mindedness, and only then
(only then)
may it be called holding fast to the name, and only then may it be called single-minded and unconfused. When the pure karma is accomplished, one goes directly to the highest grade."

O good man, the mind is originally without thought; thought pursues imagination, and this imagination is false and unreal, so one flows through birth and death. You should now know that this single phrase 'Amitabha Buddha' does not arise from imagination, does not exist from thought, dwells neither within nor without, and is without form or appearance — it is precisely to exhaust all false thinking. The Buddhas and Tathagatas are the pure, subtle, real body (the Dharma-body), neither one nor two, beyond discrimination. One who recites thus, with afflictions and dust-labor neither severed nor bound, is but the one mind. One must be single-minded, and only then may it be called holding fast to the name, and only then may it be called single-minded and unconfused. When the pure karma is accomplished, one goes directly to the highest grade."

Dingcheng bowed again and said: "I am an ordinary being of the defiled world, shallow in mind and weak in intellect, unable to reach deep into the ultimate truth. I beg you to show it more fully." The Bodhisattva said: "You should now make the great vow, vowing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; then, with utmost sincerity and compassion, call upon Amitabha Buddha. You must make the sound follow the mind and the mind follow the sound, sound and mind depending on each other, like a cat catching a mouse; sustained long without loss, you then enter the samadhi of right mindfulness. If you wish to advance further, you should widely consult good teachers and broadly seek the wise, and yourself awaken to the wondrous truth that this very mind is the Buddha. You should now possess deep faith; take care not to imitate those common, shallow people who, hearing, do not accept, and still less imitate those half-true, half-false, half-doubting, half-believing ones who, though nominally receiving it, have no sincere mind to practice it."

Gu Dingcheng bowed again and said: "I am an ordinary being of the defiled world, shallow in mind and weak in intellect, unable to reach deep into the ultimate truth. I beg the Bodhisattva to instruct me in detail." The Bodhisattva said: "You should now make the great vow, vowing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; then, with utmost sincerity and earnestness, call upon the Buddha Amitabha. You must make the sound follow the mind and the mind follow the sound, sound and mind depending on each other, like a cat catching a mouse; sustained long without loss, you then enter the samadhi of right mindfulness. If you wish to advance further, you should widely consult good teachers, broadly seek the wise, and yourself awaken to the wondrous truth of 'this very mind is the Buddha.' You should now possess deep faith; take care not to imitate those common, shallow ones who, hearing, do not accept, and still less imitate those half-true, half-false, half-doubting, half-believing ones who, though nominally receiving it, have no sincere mind to practice it."
[This mind is the Buddha]
One's own mind is originally the Buddha. (See
“A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch”

The Bodhisattva said to Madam Zha: "Why do you not recite the Buddha diligently?" She answered: "Because I have added grandchildren, and I am constantly holding and carrying them; I fear there is defilement." The Bodhisattva said: "You think that reciting the Buddha in an unclean state might bring offense, but you do not know that not reciting the Buddha brings measureless offense. Do not calculate clean and unclean; just go on reciting."

The Bodhisattva said to Madam Zha: "Why do you not recite the Buddha diligently?" Madam Zha answered: "Because I have newly added grandchildren, and I am constantly holding and carrying them; I fear there is defilement." The Bodhisattva said: "You think that reciting the Buddha in an unclean state might bring offense, but you do not know that not reciting the Buddha brings measureless offense. Do not bother reckoning clean and unclean; just keep reciting."

Chen Yongsou asked about his final destiny, and the Bodhisattva expressed it in a verse: "Moderate desire and guard against anger — this is the way to preserve the body. Withdraw and be still — this is the way to keep a household. Marry and give in marriage according to one's means — this is the way to spare oneself trouble. Practice good and recite the Buddha — this is the way to transcend the world. Uphold these four dharmas, and your final destiny will be unimpeded."

Chen Yongsou asked about his own final destiny, and the Bodhisattva instructed with a verse: "Moderate desire and guard against anger — this is the way to preserve the body. Withdraw and be still — this is the way to keep a household. Marry and give in marriage according to one's means — this is the way to spare oneself trouble. Practice good and recite the Buddha — this is the way to transcend the world. Uphold these four dharmas, and your final destiny will of itself be unimpeded."

blocks.text: A Whole Life Right or Wrong

inline.s: Gu Shanji asked about his whole life and about the method of doing good. The Bodhisattva said: "If you harbor a right mind and practice right deeds, you will gain a right whole life. If you harbor a wrong mind and practice wrong deeds, you will be given a wrong whole life. As for this one word 'good,' it can be practiced anywhere and at any time; great matters and small matters are all alike. In addition, you should also refrain from killing and release living beings, and according to your strength give to the poor and relieve suffering; hold fast to Amitabha Buddha and dedicate the merit to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, not a day broken. If you can continue thus for three years without change, only then will you be granted these four words 'a good heart doing good.'"

Gu Shanji asked how this life of his would turn out and about the method of doing good. The Bodhisattva said: "If you harbor a right mind and practice right deeds, you will gain a right whole life. If you harbor a wrong mind and practice wrong deeds, you will be given a wrong whole life. As for this one word 'good,' it can be practiced anywhere and at any time; great matters and small matters are all alike. At the same time, you should also refrain from killing and release living beings, and according to your strength give to the poor and relieve suffering; hold fast to Amitabha Buddha and dedicate the merit to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, not a day broken. If you can continue thus for three years without change, only then will you be granted these four words 'a good heart doing good.'"

The Bodhisattva instructed Wuxiu, saying: "On the whole, a person who cultivates the pure karma, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, in waking, resting, eating, and drinking, should all face the west — then the responsive resonance is easy to accomplish and the faculties and objects easy to mature. In the room, set up only one Buddha and one sutra, one censer and one table, one bed and one chair; do not place a single extra object. In the courtyard also sweep and clean thoroughly, so that walking meditation is unobstructed. Make this mind be without a single thread hanging, all the ten thousand cares forgotten, hollow and void, not knowing there is a body, not knowing there is a world, and not even knowing that what I do today is a matter of cultivation. Thus one grows daily nearer the Way and daily further from the world, and can move toward the pure karma. For when you die, if you cast off cleanly, throw away cleanly, and on the thought do not keep a single knot or rootlet, then when the great limit
(the time of death)

arrives, you will be free and easy, without making the child's clingings to body, family, and descendants — is this not the bearing of a great man? Therefore I want you to practice single-mindedly, without the least lingering attachment — it is precisely for this great key point
(the great event, meaning the arrival of the time of death)

The Bodhisattva instructed Wuxiu, saying: "On the whole, a person who cultivates the pure karma, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, in waking, resting, eating, and drinking, should all face the west — then the responsive resonance is easy to accomplish and the faculties and objects easy to mature. In the room, set up only one Buddha and one sutra, one censer and one table, one bed and one chair; do not place a single extra object. In the courtyard also sweep and clean thoroughly, so that walking meditation is unimpeded. Make this mind be without a single thread hanging, all the ten thousand cares forgotten, hollow and void, not knowing there is a body, not knowing there is a world, and not even knowing that what I do today is a matter of cultivation. Thus one grows daily nearer the Way and daily further from the world, and can move toward the pure karma. Because when you are alive you cast off cleanly and throw away cleanly, keeping not a single attachment on the thought, then when the great limit arrives you will be free and easy, without making the child's clingings to body, family, and descendants — is this not the bearing of a great man? Therefore I want you to practice single-mindedly, without the least lingering attachment — it is precisely for this great event."

"As for the method of cultivating the pure karma, it comes down to no more than these two words: single-minded and diligent. Single-minded means not directing oneself to any other matter; diligent means not wasting a single moment. Now, when you rise each morning, recite one scroll of the Amitabha Sutra, hold a thousand recitations of Amitabha Buddha, dedicate the merit before the Buddha, and recite the 'Text of Single-Minded Entrusting of Life,' because this text is simple in words yet complete in meaning. This is the lesson for one period. If at the start, or when body and mind are not yet at peace, do only four periods a day. Once somewhat at peace, gradually increase to six periods, and again gradually increase to twelve periods. That amounts to twelve scrolls of the sutra and twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name. Moreover, when dedicating the merit, the hundred prostrations to the Buddha may likewise be divided into four periods. This is the daily regular lesson. Beyond it, the recitations need not be counted; whether silent or aloud, just concentrate the mind and recite attentively."

As for the method of cultivating the pure karma, it comes down to no more than these two words: single-minded and diligent. Single-minded means not directing oneself to any other matter; diligent means not wasting a single moment. Now, when you rise each morning, you should recite one scroll of the Amitabha Sutra, hold a thousand recitations of Amitabha Buddha, dedicate the merit before the Buddha, and recite the 'Text of Single-Minded Entrusting of Life,' because this text is simple in words yet complete in meaning. This is the lesson for one period. If at the beginning, or when body and mind are not yet at peace, do only four periods a day. Once somewhat at peace, gradually increase to six periods, and again gradually increase to twelve periods. That amounts to twelve scrolls of the sutra and twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name. Moreover, when dedicating the merit, the hundred prostrations to the Buddha may likewise be divided into four periods. This is the daily regular lesson, and recitations beyond it need not be counted; whether silent or aloud, just concentrate the mind and recite attentively."

[The 'Text of Single-Minded Entrusting of Life'] "I single-mindedly entrust my life to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, to Amitabha Buddha. May he shine upon me with his pure light and embrace me with his compassionate vow. I now, in right mindfulness, call upon the name of the Tathagata, for the sake of the bodhi path, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. The Buddha's primal vow of old: if any sentient being should wish to be born in my land, and with utmost faith and joy, up to even ten recitations, should fail to be born there, may I not attain right enlightenment. Through this causal connection of Buddha-recitation, I enter the great sea of the Tathagata's vow. Relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, all offenses are eradicated and wholesome roots grow. If at the moment of death I know the time of my own coming, my body without the suffering of illness, my mind without greed or clinging, my thought unconfused, as one entering meditative concentration — the Buddha and the holy assembly, holding a golden platform in hand, come to welcome me, and in a single thought-moment I am born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. There, the flowers open and I see the Buddha, immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, at once open my Buddha-wisdom, broadly cross sentient beings, and fulfill the vow of bodhi. All Buddhas of the ten directions and three times, all bodhisattva-mahasattvas, mahaprajnaparamita."

"Again, as for the method of holding the name, you must, word by word and phrase by phrase, make sound and mind depend on each other, without mixing in the slightest worldly thought. When it matures over a long time, you will surely be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, seated on a jeweled lotus, ascending to the ground of non-retrogression. If your remaining years are not exhausted, you may still, with what you have realized, be a guide for the four assemblies, repaying the Buddha's deep grace. If you follow one and all of what I have said, then you will not fail the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing who showed you the right path and had you leave the world; nor will you fail the venerable Sanmei who shaved your head and gave you the great precepts. This is no small causal connection; do not let there arise in you a mind of slighting and neglect. Be heedful! Be heedful!"

Again, as for the method of holding the name, you must, word by word and phrase by phrase, make sound and mind depend on each other, without mixing in the slightest worldly thought. When it has matured over a long time, you will surely be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, seated on a jeweled lotus, ascending to the ground of non-retrogression. If your remaining years are not exhausted, you may still, with what you have realized, be a guide for the four assemblies, repaying the Buddha's deep grace. If you follow one and all of what I have said, then you will not fail the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing who showed you the right path and had you leave the world; nor will you fail the venerable Sanmei who shaved your head and conferred the great precepts upon you. This is no small causal connection; do not let there arise in you a mind of slighting and neglect. Be heedful! Be heedful!"

blocks.text: Advancing by Marches Both Day and Night

inline.s: The Bodhisattva instructed Changshe, saying: "You have all along
(you, all along)

held the Great Compassion Mantra, praying that Guanyin's invisible aid would speedily bring you into the Way — very good. But you must not go on delaying and procrastinating, so that your resolve and endeavor do not stand. You must work two days in one and advance by marches both day and night. From today you should fix a deadline and set an exact number of periods; cut off worldly affairs and settle in a single room. Take a hundred scrolls of the mantra as one period; together with one scroll of the repentance liturgy established by Siming
(Master Fazhi of Siming, the Great Compassion Repentance Liturgy)

, to repent all karmic hindrances and assist in giving rise to the supreme merit, as one period. Divide day and night into six periods: use five periods for the mantra, and one period for the repentance; the remaining time, sit quietly in meditation, penetrating deep into the inconceivable wisdom."

The Bodhisattva instructed Changshe, saying: "You have all along held the Great Compassion Mantra, praying that Bodhisattva Guanyin would secretly aid you to speedily enter the Way — this is very good. But you must not always be dilatory and procrastinating, so that your aspiration cannot stand. You must work two days in one and advance by marches both day and night. From today you should fix a deadline and set a set number of periods; cut off worldly affairs and settle in a single room. Take a hundred scrolls of the mantra as one period; and one scroll of the Great Compassion Repentance Liturgy, established by Master Fazhi of Siming, to repent all karmic hindrances and assist in giving rise to the supreme merit, as one period. Divide day and night into six periods: use five periods for the mantra, and one period for the repentance; the remaining time, sit quietly in meditation, penetrating deep into the inconceivable wisdom."

Why is it called the inconceivable wisdom? To know that there is no dharma outside the mind, that dharma after dharma is without name, that directly beneath, not a mote of dust stands, and that a single thought is perfect and unhindered — it cannot be thought by thinking, cannot be discussed by discussion, hence it is called the inconceivable wisdom. Relying on this wondrous wisdom, the mind is gathered in the subtle, and the gathering has no mark of gathering; the so-called gathering without anything gathered, yet not hindering the gathering — this is called well-gathering the mind. Because the mind is gathered, no matter is left undone. In a word, at no time and in no place does the mind not flow in from thought to thought — this is the root of holding the mantra and gathering the mind. Naturally the hindrances of old melt away like ice, and the concentrated mind appears clearly, or one attains the unfolding of samadhi, uniting with the original marvelous mind. Then indeed one will not idly
mí

waste the years, and can advance in the Way within a set time. Otherwise, today and tomorrow, this year and next month, if one does it and then does not, wants to go forward yet does not go forward — I guarantee that a hundred years later you will still be exactly where you are now, and you will never be able to move a single step. Be heedful! Strive!"

Why is it said to be the inconceivable wisdom? To know that there is no dharma outside the mind, that dharma after dharma is without name, that directly beneath, not a mote of dust stands, and that a single thought is perfect and unhindered — it cannot be thought by thinking, cannot be discussed by discussion, hence it is called the inconceivable wisdom. Relying on this wondrous wisdom, the mind is gathered in the subtle, and the gathering has no mark of gathering; the so-called gathering without anything gathered, yet not hindering the gathering — this is called well-gathering the mind. Because the mind is gathered, no matter is left undone. In a word, at no time and in no place does the mind not flow in from thought to thought — this is the root of holding the mantra and gathering the mind. Naturally the hindrances of old melt away like ice, and the concentrated mind appears clearly, or one attains the unfolding of samadhi, uniting with the original marvelous mind. You must by no means waste the years, but advance in the Way within a set time. Otherwise, today and tomorrow, this year and next month, if one does it and then does not, wants to go forward yet does not go forward — I guarantee that a hundred years later you will be exactly in your present state, and you will never be able to change by a single step. Be heedful! Strive!"
[Working two days in one, advancing by marches both day and night] to finish two days' work in one day, and travel two days' journey in one day.

The Bodhisattva again instructed Changshe, saying: "These eight words alone — 'forcibly yielding to human feeling, reluctantly accommodating to worldly ways' — have ruined the great matter of your whole life. Now is not a time to drag along your brothers and friends, passing the days in jest. Your practice of the Way is not yet accomplished, and impermanence arrives swiftly. You should at once conceal your traces and hide your brilliance, single-mindedly turn toward the Way, and not be mistaken again."

The Bodhisattva again instructed Changshe, saying: "These eight words alone — 'forcibly yielding to human feeling, reluctantly accommodating to worldly ways' — have ruined the great matter of your whole life. Now is not a time for dragging along your brothers and friends, laughing and jesting through the days. Your practice of the Way is not yet accomplished, and impermanence arrives swiftly. You should at once conceal your traces and hide your brilliance, single-mindedly turn toward the Way, and not be mistaken again."

[To conceal one's traces and hide one's brilliance] meaning: to be silent and invisible, and to hide one's talents. Concealing traces means not letting anyone know where one is; hiding one's brilliance means holding back one's abilities.

blocks.text: Leaving the World in Accord with the Teaching

inline.s: Daben, in accord with the teaching, left the world. The Bodhisattva instructed him, saying: "You have left the world in your old age, so you must not broadly study other matters. Just recite the Buddha's Amitabha Sutra, your daily lesson of twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name, starting from few and going to many, earnestly and sincerely, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the method of settling one matter and settling all. Do not imitate the shallow common folk of the world, who talk grandly of emptiness in high-sounding terms, speaking of nature and mind, and then, seeing a person reciting the Buddha, wipe it all away; and yet when you examine what they actually do, they fall short of an illiterate man in a village of three families, or a beggar on the crossroads reciting the Sutra of the Three Officials. You would vainly cast away your time and miss the great matter. Because you are fond of speaking of Chan but do not reach its essential mystery, and may not be able to have deep faith in the Pure Land and honestly recite the Buddha, I give you this discourse."

Daben, in accord with the teaching, left the world. The Bodhisattva instructed him, saying: "You have left the world in your old age, so you must not broadly study other matters. Just recite the Buddha's Amitabha Sutra, your daily lesson of twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name, starting from few and going to many, earnestly and sincerely, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the wondrous method of settling one matter and settling all (when the one chief matter is done, everything is in place). Do not imitate the shallow common folk of the world who talk emptily in high-sounding terms, speaking of nature and mind, and who, seeing a person reciting the Buddha, wipe it all away; and yet when you examine what they actually do, they fall short of an illiterate man in a village of three families, or a beggar on the crossroads reciting the Sutra of the Three Officials. You would vainly cast away your time and miss the great matter. Because you are fond of speaking of Chan but do not reach its essential mystery, and may not be able to have deep faith in the Pure Land and honestly recite the Buddha, I say these things to you."
[A village of three families] refers to a remote little village. [The Sutra of the Three Officials] namely the
Taishang San Yuan Ci Fu She Zui Jie E Xiao Zai Yan Sheng Bao Ming Miao Jing.

The Bodhisattva again instructed Wuxiu, saying: "Twelve scrolls of the Amitabha Sutra, twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name — do not add, do not diminish; just go by my words and practice. But the sutra should be recited evenly and purely, neither slow nor rushed, neither swift nor laggard; the Buddha's name should be recited with sound and mind in each recitation, neither rough nor dropping, neither floating nor sinking — recite up to a thousand, then dedicate the merit. When dedicating the merit, it is not merely reciting the old text through once; you must from within your own mind bring forth the true great vow of bodhi, with utmost sincerity and earnestness, universally vowing that all sentient beings be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, while my mind is attached to nothing, equal to empty space — only this is called dedication of merit."

The Bodhisattva again instructed Wuxiu, saying: "Twelve scrolls of the Amitabha Sutra, twelve thousand recitations of the Buddha's name — do not add, do not diminish; just go by my words and practice steadily. But the sutra should be recited evenly and purely, neither slow nor rushed, neither swift nor laggard; the Buddha's name should be recited with sound and mind in each recitation, neither rough nor dropping, neither floating nor sinking — recite up to a thousand, then dedicate the merit before the Buddha, reciting the 'Text of Single-Minded Entrusting of Life.' When dedicating the merit, it is not merely reciting the old text through once; you must from within your own mind bring forth the true great vow of bodhi, with utmost sincerity and earnestness, universally vowing that all sentient beings be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, while my mind is attached to nothing, equal to empty space — only this is called dedication of merit."

"Again, when sitting in meditation, you should turn inward and investigate deeply: the Buddha is my mind, this mind is the Buddha, not dependent on seeking outside; abide as the mind, with neither a subject nor an object; contemplating thus, there is no second thought — this is called cultivating samadhi. Take care not to lose your form and deaden the mind, for then you again fall into the views of an external demon. Sitting thus for one period, then rise and walk in meditation, then recite again — this has an order. If you rush hurriedly, pressing through in one breath, thinking you can finish the day's lesson, then you have a mind that merely gets it over with, and it is no longer true cultivation. On the whole, a student of the Way who does not follow the clear instruction of a good teacher will surely labor without benefit and, before long, fail. Be heedful! Be heedful!"

Take care, do not lose your form and deaden the mind, or you will again fall into the views of an external demon. Sitting thus for one period, then rise and walk in meditation, then recite — this has an order. If you rush hurriedly, pressing through in one breath, thinking you can finish the day's lesson, then you have a mind that merely gets it over with, and it is no longer true cultivation. On the whole, a student of the Way who does not follow the clear instruction of a good teacher will surely labor without benefit and, before long, fail. Be heedful! Be heedful!"

"Again, the adorned pure land of the mindfulness of the reward and the responses of which the various sutras speak must be explained and recited clearly. If, whether sitting, walking in meditation, or bowing and reciting, the Pure Land should appear before one, one can know it directly and not be confused by an alien state."

Again, the adorned pure land, both the mindfulness of the reward and the responses, of which the various sutras speak must be explained and recited clearly. If, whether sitting, or walking in meditation, or bowing and reciting, the Pure Land should appear before one, one can know it directly and not be confused by an alien state."

The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Daxin, saying: "The thought of the Way has grown in you, but the worldly thought does not diminish either. All the marks of self and others in the world, marks of name and profit, marks of anger and joy, and so on — it is not only when they issue forth from the body that they
(are)

entangled in the net of the world; even if the mind bears them ever so slightly, they are already conditions that obstruct the Way. You must understand this. You need only bow to Amitabha Buddha with your body, recite Amitabha Buddha with your mouth, and think of Amitabha Buddha with your mind, without involving the slightest other thought — then you will wash clean, break the net of the world, and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You must understand this."

The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Daxin, saying: "The thought of the Way has grown in you, but the worldly thought also does not diminish. All the marks of self and others in the world, marks of name and profit, marks of anger and joy, and so on — it is not only when they are acted out in the body that they are entangled in the net of the world; even if the mind bears them ever so slightly, they are already conditions that obstruct the Way. You must understand this. You need only bow to Amitabha Buddha with your body, recite Amitabha Buddha with your mouth, and think of Amitabha Buddha with your mind, without involving the slightest other thought — then you will wash clean, break the net of the world, and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You must understand this principle."

blocks.text: One Asks about One's Whole Life

inline.s: Someone asked about his whole life. The Bodhisattva said: "You ask about your whole life? I have here no method for determining a whole life, because the Bodhisattva, in practicing through kalpa after kalpa, never learned such a matter. Yet you are indeed too foolish: a whole life is no more than this, so what is the use of asking about it? Why do you not ask, when your head has turned white, your face has wrinkled, your body has grown weak, and impermanence is about to arrive, how you are to face King Yama with a single half-sentence, so as to avoid going off in shackles and chains? Why do you not ask about this matter?"

Someone asked about his whole life. The Bodhisattva said: "You ask about your whole life? I have no method here for determining a whole life, because the Bodhisattva, in practicing through kalpa after kalpa, never learned such fortune-telling. Yet you are indeed too foolish: a whole life is no more than this, so what is the use of asking about it? Why do you not ask, when your head has turned white, your face has wrinkled, your body has grown weak, and impermanence is about to arrive, how before King Yama you are to match him with a single half-sentence, so as to avoid going off in shackles and chains? Why do you not ask about this matter?"
[Asking about one's whole life, asking about one's final destiny]

The true answer to asking about one's whole life and asking about one's final destiny is this: though a little poorer, a little more ill, a little more frustrated, a little shorter-lived — as long as at death one is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then the whole life is a good whole life, and that final destiny is a blissful final destiny. Conversely, though somewhat richer, healthier, smoother, longer-lived — if at death one cannot be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then the whole life is a bad whole life, and that final destiny is a miserable final destiny. Therefore, rather than care about poverty or wealth, sickness or health, adversity or ease, an early or a late death, it is better to care about how to recite the Buddha well. And moreover, poverty or wealth, sickness or health, adversity or ease, an early or a late death are often beyond one's control, whereas whether one recites the Buddha well lies within my own grasp. So to recite the Buddha well is the wondrous method that settles everything once and for all; over the rest there is no need to be too concerned.
